name: Ngemba (Bamoungoum)
place: Bamoungoum paramount chiefdom, Bafoussam III (Mifi, West)
overview: Founded by a hunter in search of land, the Bamoungoum kingdom, the majority in its area, welcomes Hausa, people from Mbouda, Bansoa and Bamoun. A chiefdom structured around notables and protective secret societies, ancestor and skull worship, the refuge cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ: every two years, for four months, the Bamoungoum celebrate their great festival Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, in contact with the Hausa, Mbouda, Bansoa and the Bamoun; some also speak their languages.
Ŋgəmba is spoken throughout Cameroon, with the diaspora.
Mostly indigenous population, but with mixed marriages; women more often marry outside the group. Formerly, it was unacceptable for a Bamoungoum son to ally himself with another group.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: The founders found this land and made it their ancestral land, charged with religious meaning.
Having come from Bansoa, they remain tied to it: when the Bamoungoum chief dies, it is the chief of Bansoa who enthrones his successor.
An old land dispute still pits the Bamoungoum against the Bameka.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: A well-structured chiefdom, with its notables; the former castes and the passing down of trades from father to son have declined.
The chief decides after consulting his notables.
Succession goes from father to son; if a clan has no boy, a member of another clan may inherit.
The chiefdom's secret societies, hereditary, protect and purify the people and drive out evil spirits.
One stands up when a notable arrives and waits for his seat to “cool down” before sitting in it. Formerly, a distance was kept from the in-laws.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband's family.
The boy becomes a man when he takes care of himself or leaves the family home.
Steps: “knocking at the door”, introduction to the suitor's family, handing over then checking of the list, customary marriage.
Raffia wine, cola and oil seal the alliance.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Ancestor cult performed by the family elders, according to circumstances, from a personal problem to a collective crisis.
Sacred places: the cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ (“house of the walk”), a refuge during wars and a place of memory; the ŋgwo'ŋgon, a place of justice where abnormal events are judged by a ritual ordeal.
A birth can be a reincarnation, recognised by signs left on a deceased child; death is a return to the forebears.
The dead are consulted in succession disputes or when their word has not been respected; failing to respect a will brings a curse.
Taboos: incest (cause of sterility), adultery, any familiarity with the chief's wife, theft.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Formerly coffee and tobacco; today trade and farming.
The land belongs to the chief; it is obtained mainly by inheritance.
Ancestral crafts: dance masks, clay pots, vases and calabashes for sacred places.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The ndop is the ceremonial dress, including for queens.
Diviners and skulls, and traditional medicine, are consulted first, before the hospital in serious cases.
Beauty is moral: good manners, respect, values; the family's reputation matters more than appearance.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: mûŋgù, sàmàlí, yuutə', njə̀mâsà, lálí; instruments: drum, castanets, balafon.
The sàmàlí is danced at funerals; the lálí, a ritual dance, at the mourning of queen mothers.
Festival: Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum, lasting four months, in odd-numbered years.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Political organisation, ancestor worship and the way justice is administered bring the Bamoungoum close to the Bamoun.

sections.title: The names
items: Ta- marks men's names, ma- women's.
No naming rite, except for twins, who receive the names of the last two chiefs.
One changes name if the child grows poorly; terms of deference: ncia (elder), pa-, ma-; ndi for the greatness of a notable; the chief (pfə̌) is addressed by saying mə̀tɛ̌.
The founder, Fɛndzɔnveu, was a hunter.

lessons.title: Who are the Ngemba (Bamoungoum)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition

vocabulary.frenchText: Hill that separates the bameka and the bamoungoum
<watercourse referring to a notable called fotsing>

lessons.competence: Introduce the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, in contact with the Hausa, Mbouda, Bansoa and the Bamoun; some also speak their languages. • Ŋgəmba is spoken everywhere in Cameroon, together with the diaspora. • Mostly native population, but mixed marriages; women marry outside the group more often. In the past, it was unacceptable for a Bamoungoum son to ally himself with another group. • The founders found this land and made it their ancestral land, charged with religious meaning. • Having come from Bansoa, they remain tied to it: when the Bamoungoum chief dies, it is the chief of Bansoa who enthrones his successor.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Founded by a hunter in search of land, the Bamoungoum kingdom, the majority in its area, welcomes Hausa, people from Mbouda, Bansoa and Bamoun. A chiefdom structured around notables and protective secret societies, ancestor and skull worship, the refuge cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ: every two years, for four months, the Bamoungoum celebrate their great festival Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.competence: Describe how the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Ngemba (Bamoungoum) village. Who decides, and how?

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Ngemba (Bamoungoum) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

In the past, a distance was kept from the in-laws.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)

lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.

lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: maize couscous (mə̀nsáŋ), ŋkwǐ greens, banana fufu, pounded. • Drinks: raffia wine. • Formerly coffee and tobacco; today trade and farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Ngemba (Bamoungoum) mainly eat mə̀nsáŋ, ŋkwǐ vegetables, banana fufu, pounded dishes. Traditional drinks: raffia wine. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Taking part in cultural life in the family and in society: the class is preparing a Ngemba (Bamoungoum) dance performance for cultural day.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Which dances are practised, and on what occasions? — Who dances (men, women, children, initiates)? When and where? — Which instruments, songs and outfits are used? — What is the cultural meaning of the chosen dance?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Rhythms: mûŋgù, sàmàlí, yuutə', njə̀mâsà, lálí; instruments: drum, castanets, balafon. • The sàmàlí is danced at funerals; the lálí, a ritual dance, at the mourning of queen mothers. • Festival: Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum, lasting four months, in odd-numbered years.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), traditional dances (funerals, mourning of queen mothers) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, castanets, balafon. Festival(s): Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Describe a Ngemba (Bamoungoum) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

student.memo: Among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), traditional dances (funerals, mourning of queen mothers) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: drum, castanets, balafon. Festival(s): Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Ngemba (Bamoungoum). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Ngemba (Bamoungoum). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following elements: • In the past coffee and tobacco; today trade and crops. • The land belongs to the chief; it is obtained mainly by inheritance. • Ancestral crafts: dance masks, canaris, vases and calabashes for sacred places.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Formerly coffee and tobacco; today trade and crops. The land belongs to the chief; it is mainly obtained by inheritance.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Ancestor worship led by the family elders, according to circumstances, from a personal problem to a collective crisis. • Sacred places: the cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ (“house of the walk”), a refuge during wars and a place of memory; the ŋgwo'ŋgon, a place of justice where abnormal events are judged by a ritual ordeal. • A birth may be a reincarnation, recognised by signs left on a deceased child; death is a return to the ancestors. • The dead are consulted in succession disputes or when their word has not been respected; failing to respect a will brings a curse. • Taboos: incest (a cause of sterility), adultery, any familiarity with the chief's wife, theft.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Ancestor worship is conducted by the family elders, depending on the circumstances, from a personal problem to a collective crisis. Sacred places: the cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ (“house of the walk”), a refuge during wars and a place of memory; the ŋgwo'ŋgon, a place of justice where abnormal events are judged by a ritual ordeal.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Ŋgəmba
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Ngemba (Bamoungoum) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Ngemba (Bamoungoum) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Ngemba (Bamoungoum) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Ŋgəmba. • Greeting formulas: Mə̌tsa’ tsə̀ = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Ózīa óljà = morning greeting (one person); Pʉlja = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: [mɔ̌?], [pà], [tə́t], [kwa], [tɛ]. • The founder, Fɛndzɔnveu, was a hunter. • Political organisation, ancestor worship and the way justice is rendered bring the Bamoungoum closer to the Bamoun.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Ŋgəmba are the first steps towards communicating with the Ngemba (Bamoungoum). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Ŋgəmba.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.
